utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Could I have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Katrina Gustafson, Ann Sutherland, Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, and Iain Reid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. Yes, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Excellencies. Good day to everyone in the courtroom. On behalf of the Defence, we are present here today; myself and my legal advisor, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. First, I recall that the Chamber, in its decision of 11th of June, 2014, made it clear that, as far as a Status Conference is concerned, Rule 65 bis (A) purported to apply to the pre-trial stage of the proceedings and that this had been confirmed by the consistent practice of the other Trial Chambers which had not convened Status Conferences after the start of trial, including during periods in which the accused person had not appeared before those Chambers for more than 120 days. Next, I recall that on the 9th of December, 2014, the accused requested that the Chamber hold a Status Conference to discuss the Prosecution disclosure practices and matters relating to his health and the conditions of his detention. On the 8th of January, 2015, the Chamber found that the -- the Chamber granted the request, in part, and decided that a Status Conference should be held today but only to address health and conditions of detention. The Chamber found that the Prosecution's disclosure obligations had been highly litigated in this case and that there was no specific issue not addressed in writing which warranted the holding of a Status Conference. That said, Mr. Karadzic, the floor is now yours in relation to your health and detention. If at any time you wish to move into private session, let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I have decided to speak here about matters that I'm unable to resolve with the management of the Detention Unit with whom I have very professional co-operation in matters that they are able to decide on. However, some things are systemic, they don't depend on them but evidently depend on something else. First of all, I believe that you have it. I authorised the medical service to report to you about all my health and lab test results. And, as you can see, I came here in perfect health with perfect test results and all other parameters were excellent. All of that, not only is it no longer so but is far below perfect, and you can see that for yourself in the test results. Mostly it refers to blood sugar. This is not the case just in -- in my case, but it applies to others as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you continue, I wanted to let you know that the Trial Chamber hasn't received any report about your medical condition. But please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The medical service asked me, and I did sign the authorisation that they can send all my test results to you. So, in my case and in the case of other detainees, there is a problem with the metabolising of sugar. This is something that has cropped up. It's quite serious. I don't believe this is an error of the service. I believe that perhaps it could be a matter of food or the entire system. Then there is also another matter, and it's a -- very many cases of malignant diseases, and the percentage among 100 of the detainees is equal to that of the percentage among hundreds of thousands. So it's a bit unusual to have so many malignant diseases if we compare it to the usual occurrence of such cases. Perhaps it has something to do with the food, it has something do with the circumstances of detention, or the health of the building, and I think this is a matter that somebody would need to investigate and take a position on. We would need to pay attention to that and see what the possible causes are. This is as far as my health is concerned. As far as other matters are concerned, I also wanted to bring up other things that I could not resolve with the management of the Detention Unit. I would like to say that the Trial Chamber and the President, in a number of times, granted my requests relating to respect of my rights for certain means, for communication with the media. All these matters were resolved. I'm a professional, first of all, I'm a doctor. I'm also an author. I don't know how long I will be staying here and in what status, and I now have more time because, up until now, until we finished our presentation of the case, I devoted all my time to the Defence and to keeping my head above the water, so to say. But now I have more time. I have time to work on the -- using the Internet, to work with audio-recording devices because I wanted to work on my language skills. The Serbian language has been reformed since my forbearers spoke it. I think there are a lot of things that I still need to do in order to make sure that the use of that language is correct. I know that there were people who defended themselves after being provisionally released or were I, by any chance, on provisional release until the Judgement, I would not have such restrictions. However, my access to Internet, to the Internet, which is monitored, should only have limitations in my communications with others, but in my access to material from the Internet should not be restricted in any way, and detention should not imply any restrictions that do not have any kind of punitive nature. If I were Seselj and spent 12 years here and not be able to professionally be active, I believe that all of these are punitive measures which are unsuitable for a civilised world. So as far as Internet is concerned, I would like to be able to record the correct pronunciation of the Serbian. There are 400.000 words, there are seven conjugations, meaning that there are 2 million words that need to be recorded, properly pronounced. So this is another matter I would like to have to resolved. I apologise to the interpreters. I absolutely accept any kind of monitoring. I don't have a habit of breaking any rules, so I would accept any kind of monitoring that has to do with the work of the Tribunal and the security in the Detention Unit. However, there is enough leeway there for a professional to work without bringing anything into jeopardy. I would also like to say that the ICC also has its own detention facilities in the same building. The conditions are different. They're more liberal. They're better; particularly in terms of food than is the case in our Detention Unit. So I ask myself whether the Tribunal would need be to informed about the fact that two courts of the same United Nations do not have the same conditions. This would be useful and a good thing to draw the Tribunal's attention so that the conditions could be the same in both DU units. I would also like to say that all of us who are there are very much concerned about the convicted persons from the Balkans are being sent to serve their sentences in former Communist countries and in countries where the conditions of detention are very much different from the conditions in countries in the EU. We would perhaps prefer for them to serve their sentences in more progressive European countries because all of that contributes to the bitterness of the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We won't go there. That's beyond the issues the Trial Chamber can discuss at the moment. As to the items you referred, including your medical problem and the other several conditions of detention, I'm not sure at this moment what role that this Trial Chamber can play. So I would like you to liaise with the detention authorities, including medical officer, and raise issues with them and then discuss and then come back to the Chamber, if necessary, when your fair trial right is infringed. Mr. Robinson, would you like to add anything in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Actually, Dr. Karadzic has corresponded with the commander of the Detention Unit on these issues and has also been dealing with the medical officer on these issues, but he thought it was important that the Trial Chamber be informed, although he is not asking you to take any action, but part of the reason for the Status Conference was to keep you informed on his health and on his conditions of detention, and that's the purpose of his intervention this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the answer to this may be something that you want to put into a private session; that's entirely a matter for you. But the question that concerns me is this: Any of the medical conditions that you've alluded to, or the medical situation to put it broadly that you have alluded to, are they causing you actual distress or symptoms of a debilitating nature?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, no. It's not an acute situation but my health has deteriorated; in particular, my blood sugar level. And I'm not the only one. There are quite of number of us in the meantime who have -- are started to suffer from diabetes. I was in excellent health, so I'm afraid that perhaps it is not just that metabolic aspect that is in question. There could be some other consequences that could appear a bit later. We are receiving food that is frozen, that is heated in microwaves, in plastic containers. Paracetamol is a medicine that we use in the DU as much as we want. However, the latest research indicates that Paracetamol is quite dangerous. So there are these systemic matters that do not depend on the people who are there. Simply, the system of detention of the United Nations is producing illnesses among many people. This is the main point. If you look at my test results when I arrived, they were quite perfect, and then each successive one was worse, and the consequences of this have still to appear. Of course, I can still work and do my job, but the state of my health is not good. And I don't want to mention without their permission the names of people who in the meantime are now ill with diabetes or have some malignant disease. All I am saying is that all these things would indicate that the Tribunal would need to look into all of these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber has noted the information Mr. Karadzic has raised. Are there any other issues?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I wanted to say is that the question of my rights, or my right to work in my profession, being monitored, of course, is -- while in detention is something that cannot be resolved without a clear position from the Tribunal. I cannot expect the DU management to resolve all of these questions regarding access to the Internet and the recording of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. There is a regime in place to deal with the various detention issues as well as health problems. The Chamber will look into the matters when required. Unless there's other issues, there's one matter the Chamber wishes to deal with at this moment in private session. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless there's a further matter to raise, hearing is now adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
